A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Adv-BMT research work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison after matching renamed variants and relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original motion-prediction, adversarial-generation, and reinforcement-learning experiments in Section 4, plus WOSAC results in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and additionally reports component ablations in Appendix C.1, Tables 9–10.

M1.justification: v2 adds an explicit Adv-BMT mode that removes teacher-forcing and jointly reconstructs all agents backward, whereas v1 places entirely new scenario reconstruction outside its scope. This extends the inference procedure using the existing BMT. Tokenization, architecture, losses, filtering, and optional forward refinement are otherwise retained; forward refinement is not new.

E1.justification: WOMD, MetaDrive, motion prediction, and downstream RL remain the principal coverage. v2 Figure 6 explicitly demonstrates pedestrian and cyclist adversaries, extending the vehicle-only adversarial scope stated in v1's limitations. v1 already mentions these agent types in training and mixed-agent demos, so this is a limited expansion of demonstrated adversarial coverage.

E2.justification: The competing methods remain CAT, STRIVE, and SEAL for scenario generation and open-loop RL, and CAT for closed-loop RL. The unaugmented Waymo training reference also remains. Newly cited diffusion methods are not evaluated baselines; changes among BMT configurations concern internal ablations.

E3.justification: The evaluation design is substantially revised: Table 1 removes the one-second-history condition and expands collision and distributional metrics; Table 2 compares replayed versus jointly predicted traffic with and without filtering. Time-to-collision JSD is added. WOSAC is described as 2025 rather than 2024, although unchanged scores do not establish reevaluation. The main RL protocol remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds controlled comparisons of teacher-forcing and filtering in Table 2, and isolates adversarial initialization and filtering in Appendix C.1, Tables 9–10. These directly examine central components beyond v1's forward-refinement comparison. v2 also adds a qualitative investigation attributing many reverse-prediction collision detections to crowded parking areas.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight random seeds for RL and retain the same plus/minus reporting in the corresponding tables. v2 adds no confidence intervals, significance tests, or additional repeated-run information for the revised generation results or new ablations.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 substantially replace prediction and generation results, and v2 adds ablation outcomes. For example, STRIVE's reported attack-success value changes from 0.534 to 0.38; revised settings prevent interpreting this as a same-setting performance change. RL and WOSAC numerical results remain unchanged. The generation-time table changes Adv-BMT from 0.74 to 1.02 seconds, matching v1's existing main-text value.

T1.justification: v1's explicit mean contour-distance definition and argmin token-selection equation, Eq. 4, are omitted; v2 retains only qualitative contour-matching descriptions. Most dynamics and training mathematics remain in Appendix A. Rewriting likelihood maximization as negative-log-likelihood minimization is equivalent, and neither version supplies theoretical proofs.

C1.justification: The three headline contributions and collision-free pretraining claim remain. v2's introduction and conclusion broaden the stated capability to jointly synthesized, reactive multi-agent scenes. The abstract retains the 20% collision-reduction claim but removes its explicit comparison with previous work.

C2.justification: v1 interprets bidirectional prediction as harming accuracy and acknowledges a baseline-realism versus diversity tradeoff; v2 instead emphasizes improved bidirectional accuracy and Adv-BMT realism. It adds filtering mechanisms, parking-lot collision explanations, and stronger causal interpretations of RL benefits. The vehicle-only limitation is replaced by computational-resource demands, while limited downstream validation remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: The abstract changes a promised code release to stated availability of code and demos. v2 additionally specifies dataset frequency, maximum agent count, and prediction-sequence length. Hardware, model parameters, and most hyperparameters remain unchanged. Its new approximately 800,000-step pretraining account conflicts with the retained one-million-step description in Appendix A.4.

R1.justification: v2 adds a short diffusion-literature discussion citing MotionDiffuser, SceneControl, Scenario Diffusion, and other methods, and adds DenseTNT when describing CAT. It removes MixSim and several dataset-format citations, and withdraws the statement that SafeSim requires collision training data. These update positioning without replacing the overall research framing.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work, method exposition, and result discussions are extensively rewritten. Section 3 is reorganized from five subsections into three, with more explanatory prose, while Appendix A gains separate decoding and training subsections. This substantially changes the narrative structure beyond accommodating new experiments.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the overview and architecture diagrams, adds third-person and pedestrian/cyclist illustrations, restructures Tables 1–2, and adds ablation tables. The baseline-comparison figure loses one example row. Some displays are retained and relocated: v1 Figures 4 and 6 correspond to v2 Figures 5 and 8, respectively.

improvement.justification: The added component ablations and clearer descriptions of generation modes make central design choices better supported and easier to assess. These gains are partly offset by reporting problems: v2 claims forward refinement lowers episode cost although unchanged Table 4 shows 1.35 increasing to 1.39, and it adds a conflicting pretraining count. The net improvement is therefore limited.
